strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect the outputs of interactive qualitative coding systems. This is a worthwhile empirical contribution to pursue.

The study involves substantial empirical work: 20 participants and 15 coding sessions across three different system families on a shared corpus of approximately 85,000 tweets. Fixed initializations within each system improve comparability.

The evaluation combines consistency, semantic cohesion and separation, manual assessment of 1,200 document–theme pairs, and participant interviews. Double annotation with adjudication and reported agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha = 0.632) provide useful evidence beyond automated metrics. The system descriptions and evaluation dimensions are generally clearly presented.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Section 4 compares individual codebooks with codebooks produced by three-person groups. Although asynchronous collaboration is defined as independent work followed by consolidation, no consolidation stage is evaluated. Differences therefore also reflect team size and aggregation of perspectives. The paper needs either an appropriate asynchronous collaborative comparison or narrower claims about individual versus joint coding.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified. Each system has only two synchronous sessions and three individual sessions. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying their observational units or explaining dependencies among themes within codebooks and comparisons sharing coders. Theme-level observations cannot substitute for independent session replication. Sample sizes, exact p-values, uncertainty estimates, and treatment of multiple comparisons are needed before accepting the claims of significant collaboration effects.

The correctness evaluation has important reporting inconsistencies. Figure 4 reports F1, but the described audit only judges assigned document–theme pairs; the construction of false negatives and the averaging procedure are unexplained. The claim that asynchronous topic modeling produces more accurate assignments also conflicts with the figure: it performs better only in the closest quartile, worse at the next two cumulative thresholds, and equally overall. Confidence intervals and the treatment of invalid LLM labels, affecting 0.7–16.1% of documents in Table 4, are missing.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger validation and specification. Per-theme maximum similarity can conceal many-to-one correspondences and is sensitive to theme granularity. Final theme counts, sizes, and precise matching and aggregation rules are not reported. Centroid similarities of 0.94–0.98 offer limited discrimination, and the paper does not establish that changes in these proxies correspond to substantively better themes.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendices. Participant allocation and reuse, session order and duration, the evaluation embedding checkpoint, selected prompt for each codebook, and decoding settings are unspecified. Codebooks, annotations, and analysis code are described as a future release. Appendix C also acknowledges missing interviews without reporting completion counts by condition or a systematic interview-analysis procedure.

Several recommendations exceed the evidence. Differences among three complete systems do not establish that interaction bandwidth causes greater benefits from deliberation; their supervision and inference mechanisms also differ. Broad conclusions about LLM reliability and expense rely on one 3B model and one inference setup. Restricting these claims, resolving the experimental comparison, and correcting the analyses could support a next-cycle resubmission, but the current validity and reproducibility gaps prevent a positive Findings recommendation.
